comparison: Both strongly support the in vitro APP gene upregulation findings (C1-C9). OpenEval emphasizes dose-dependent effects and cross-validation across cell lines. Peer reviewers describe the in vitro mechanistic data as 'compelling' and 'solid' with no concerns raised. Both also address MHC-I protein expression (C10-C12 in OpenEval, included in peer R1).

OpenEval R2 focuses specifically on MHC-I protein expression (C10-C12), while peer R1 includes these claims as part of their broader acceptance of in vitro findings. Both evaluations support the translation from mRNA to functional protein expression.

Both support the metabolomic evidence for DHODH inhibition (C13-C16). OpenEval emphasizes the rapid kinetics and dose-dependence. Peer reviewers accept the metabolomics data and confirm target engagement both in vitro and in vivo (including C98-C103).

Both strongly support the uridine rescue experiments demonstrating pyrimidine depletion as the causal mechanism (C17-C31). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of specificity across cell lines. Peer reviewers accept that the effect 'is mediated strictly by pyrimidine depletion' and also include genetic validation with DHODH knockout cells (C34-C37).

OpenEval R5 focuses on genetic validation with DHODH knockout cells (C32-C37). Peer R3 includes these claims as part of their broader acceptance of the pyrimidine depletion mechanism, noting the genetic validation is not questioned.

Perfect agreement on the specificity screen (C40-C44). Both support the finding that only nucleotide synthesis inhibitors induce APP genes, arguing against nonspecific stress responses. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Both support the independence from canonical APP pathways (C46-C48). OpenEval emphasizes this establishes a novel mechanism. Peer reviewers accept the pathway independence findings and specifically note the evidence for interferon signaling independence, also including IKK2 knockout validation (C55-C62).

OpenEval R8 addresses BMS-345541 and IKK2 independence (C49-C62). Peer R5 includes the IKK2 knockout validation claims as part of their acceptance of pathway independence findings. Both support these conclusions without concerns.

Both address CDK9/P-TEFb involvement (C63-C72), but with different levels of certainty. OpenEval finds the pharmacological evidence compelling and sufficient. Peer reviewers find it 'convincing' but explicitly request genetic validation (CRISPR KO, shRNA), identifying reliance solely on pharmacological tools as a limitation.

OpenEval R10 provides detailed support for CDK9 requirement using PROTAC validation (C73-C84). Peer R6 includes these claims but still requests additional genetic validation beyond the PROTAC approach, suggesting the mechanistic confirmation remains incomplete without direct genetic depletion.

Both address the transcriptional mechanism (C85-C89), but with different levels of certainty. OpenEval finds the ChIP-seq and kinetics data compelling. Peer reviewers request additional validation, noting the reliance on published ChIP-seq data from a single locus (HLA-B) is insufficient and requesting heatmaps across more loci to substantiate the mechanistic claim.

Both support the in vivo tumor growth suppression and metabolomic validation (C95-C104). OpenEval emphasizes the translation of in vitro findings. Peer reviewers accept the efficacy and APP induction data without questioning tumor growth suppression or molecular changes.

OpenEval R12 includes in vivo metabolomics (C98-C103) as part of tumor model validation. Peer R2 accepts these metabolomics data as confirming target engagement in vivo. Both evaluations support this evidence.

Major disagreement on combination therapy interpretation (C105-C112). OpenEval finds proof-of-concept evidence for therapeutic benefit with sequential administration superior to concurrent. Peer reviewers challenge whether APP induction actually contributed to ICB efficacy, request immune cell depletion experiments, note the response appears additive rather than synergistic, and question whether the title claim is supported. Editor concludes in vivo functional assessments remain incomplete.

OpenEval R13 includes in vivo efficacy claims (C105, C110-C111) as part of survival benefit evidence. Peer R8 accepts the basic in vivo efficacy data but peer R9 challenges the mechanistic interpretation of combination effects.

OpenEval R14 supports the authors' summary conclusions (C113-C118, C146-C147) as well-supported by comprehensive evidence. Peer R1 includes C113 in their acceptance of in vitro findings but does not evaluate the broader summary claims.
OpenEval R14 includes summary claims about pyrimidine depletion dependence (C114-C115). Peer R3 accepts the underlying mechanistic evidence for these claims.
OpenEval R14 includes summary claim about pathway independence (C116). Peer R5 accepts the underlying evidence for this conclusion.

OpenEval R14 includes summary claim about CDK9 requirement (C117). Peer R6 finds the pharmacological evidence convincing but requests genetic validation, suggesting uncertainty about the strength of this conclusion.
OpenEval R14 includes summary claim about transcriptional mechanism (C146). Peer R7 requests additional validation of the transcriptional mechanism, suggesting the evidence is incomplete.

Both support the TCGA survival correlation analysis (C92). OpenEval notes it is correlative and does not establish causation. Peer reviewers accept this bioinformatic finding without challenge as supporting context for therapeutic relevance.

Both support the clinical application hypothesis for interferon pathway-defective tumors (C119-C121). OpenEval notes this remains a hypothesis requiring validation. Peer reviewers specifically requested this discussion point and accept the independence from interferon signaling as demonstrated.
OpenEval R16 includes the clinical application claim (C119). Peer R9 challenges the broader combination therapy interpretation but does not specifically address the interferon pathway hypothesis.

OpenEval R17 addresses discrepancies with prior literature regarding ATM and cGAS-STING-TBK1 pathways (C131-C135), finding the authors' interpretation reasonable. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval R18 supports the discussion of treatment scheduling implications (C138-C141). Peer R9 includes C141 in their broader challenge of the combination therapy interpretation, questioning whether the data support the claimed synergy.
OpenEval R19 supports the authors' acknowledgment of limitations regarding thymidylate synthase inhibitors (C142-C145). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval R20 addresses established biological knowledge claims including ICB as melanoma therapy (C93). Peer R11 includes C93 in their acceptance of the TCGA analysis context. Both treat these as appropriate background information.
OpenEval R20 includes established knowledge about P-TEFb (C41). Peer R4 includes C41 in their acceptance of the specificity screen findings. Both treat this as appropriate context.
OpenEval R21 addresses citations to prior work including S2-013 resistance (C6). Peer R1 includes C6 in their acceptance of the in vitro findings. Both treat these as appropriate scientific context.

OpenEval R21 addresses multiple citations to prior work (C32-C33, C90-C91, C94, C122-C128) establishing scientific context. No specific peer review evaluation found for most of these citation claims, though some overlap with accepted findings.

OpenEval R22 identifies speculative statements (C129, C136-C137, C148) as uncertain, noting they represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these speculative claims.
